title: The main defence: 6...Kxf7 7.Nf3 c5!
outcomes: Says what 7...c5 attacks (the pawn on d4) and counts attackers and defenders of d4 before and after White's extra defender
Lists White's checks first and answers each (the pawn block on e6, the king to g8 after the knight check)

Counts the guards of e6 and the retakers of d4 before choosing a move in the main line, and tells a queen capture that works from one that does not
Says why Black stays clearly better in the main line and what Black must still avoid

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** White has paid a knight for one pawn, but the black king is exposed. Which move does Black play now, and how does Black meet White's checks and tries without handing the extra piece back? By the end you can say why 7...c5 is a good move, answer each of White's four tries, and name what Black must still avoid. Marks: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.caption: The engine (depth 16) puts ...c5 first; at depth 20 ...e6 ties with it, and ...Be6 and ...Bf5 are close behind. We study ...c5 because it also attacks d4 with tempo. [V] All of these leave Black clearly better, so the question is which move meets White's plans best, not which one avoids disaster.

steps.text: **Why only about two pawns?** [V] White has seven pawns, Black six, and Black has the extra knight: a knight for a pawn is worth about two pawns on the usual counting scale, and the engine agrees. [I] White's compensation is practical: the king on f7 cannot castle, checks keep coming, and Black's queenside pieces are still at home. [H] Every move Black plays should shrink one of those three problems.

steps.text: **Count the checks first.** A check cuts down your choices, so it decides what you may play next. [H] When your king is exposed, list the checks before your own wishes. When there are only a few, you can calculate every line to the end, and that is Black's job in this lesson.

**The idea of 7...c5.** [I] The pawn on d4 is White's only central pawn. The move hits it at once, and the queen already looks at it down the open d-file. It also frees c6 for the b8 knight, so a single pawn move does three jobs.

steps.caption: The pawn move hits d4. Count the pieces on each side of that pawn after the move.

Two white pieces defend d4: the knight and the queen.

steps.text: **What the count means.** Two attackers against two defenders: neither side can simply win the pawn by capturing. [H] So the details around d4 decide the line: a third white defender holds the pawn, and a white piece that leaves d4's reach loses a defender. The next contrast changes one thing at a time.

steps.text: **One pattern behind four tries.** [V] Each White try, whether a check, a pawn push or a capture, leaves Black clearly better at depth 16. [I] White never has time for two ideas at once: every extra move costs a tempo that the exposed black king would need. The quiet developing moves do not change the verdict either.

**The main line, move by move.** [I] Black's plan: block the check with the pawn, win the d4 pawn when it is safe, bring the knight to c6, and keep e6 defended. The board shows each step with its purpose. Watch the counts on e6 and d4: they decide which moves are safe.

steps.text: **Why Black is better, and what keeps Black better.** [I] The extra piece is real; the white pieces point at e6, d4 and the king, but each target is defended or can be. What Black must do is simple: keep e6 guarded, develop the pieces, and get the king to a quiet square. The next boards show what Black must not do.

steps.text: **Recap.** [V] After 7.Nf3 Black is clearly better in all four tries. Count the checks first. Strike at d4 with a pawn. Block with the pawn, not the bishop. After a knight check the king goes to the corner. Count the defenders of e6 and d4 before capturing or moving a piece. A queen does not take where a knight can retake.
